key_points.point: The document argues that transparency is a necessary public good to promote competition and ensure corporate governance. By defining indicators and collating reports, the authors aim to buttress industry standards and norms, which aligns with the accelerationist goal of creating a transparent, competitive market environment. The authors note that transparency is currently low and heterogeneous, suggesting that standardized reporting could help level the playing field for developers.
key_points.verbatim: Transparency about how AI companies operate is necessary to ensure corporate governance, mitigate societal harms from AI, and promote competition. ... By quantifying and comparing the practices of these companies, we expect it will contribute towards advancing transparency, both through the direct engagement with these companies and the indirect support of other agents of change (e.g. policymakers, journalists, clients, consumers, investors).

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that foundation model architectures are evolving beyond vanilla transformers, necessitating more granular transparency into model properties. This shift reflects the accelerationist belief that AI capabilities are rapidly advancing and diversifying, requiring new frameworks to track progress. The document's focus on 'test-time scaling' and 'reasoning models' highlights the ongoing expansion of AI's problem-solving utility.
key_points.verbatim: However, foundation model architectures have also, over time, deviated from vanilla transformers/diffusion-models (Groeneveld et al., 2024), creating a need for transparency into properties of models beyond high-level descriptions of architecture or components.

key_points.point: The document advocates for a transparency framework that relies on disclosure-based metrics to foster market-driven accountability. By standardizing reporting across diverse developers, including international firms, it aims to create a competitive environment where transparency becomes a differentiator. This approach prioritizes market-based incentives over rigid, top-down mandates, aligning with the goal of enabling innovation while maintaining visibility into the ecosystem.
key_points.verbatim: By diversifying the companies, the 2025 FMTI provides a more comprehensive view of global transparency practices.

key_points.point: The document highlights that open-weight developers like IBM demonstrate the potential for third-party innovation by releasing code that allows others to train and run models. This supports the accelerationist goal of democratizing access to cognitive tools. However, the document notes that even among open-weight developers, there are significant limits to operationalizing these benefits, suggesting that mere openness is not yet sufficient for full democratization.
key_points.verbatim: IBM is the only company to release code that allows third parties to train and run the model, demonstrating the limits—even among open-weight developers—in operationalizing the benefits from fully open-source software

key_points.point: The document argues that transparency indexes serve as mechanisms to shape corporate behavior and improve incentives. By creating a standardized, public-facing measurement of transparency, the index encourages companies to compete on openness, which can drive better alignment with public interest. This approach leverages market-based transparency to foster a more robust and accountable AI ecosystem without necessarily requiring heavy-handed state intervention.
key_points.verbatim: Under this view, the Foundation Model Transparency Index belongs not only to the class of measurement instruments used to study AI companies, but also the class of mechanisms used to shape AI companies.

key_points.point: The document references extensive research on data licensing and provenance, which accelerationists interpret as the necessary infrastructure for scaling AI. By documenting the shift toward formal licensing deals (e.g., Reddit, News Corp), the text highlights the transition from open-web scraping to structured, proprietary data access. This supports the accelerationist goal of securing high-quality data pipelines to sustain model performance improvements.
key_points.verbatim: Kyle Wiggers. Shutterstock expands deal with OpenAI to build generative AI tools. 2023. URL https://techcrunch.com/2023/07/11/shutterstock-expands-deal-with-openai-to-build-generative-ai-tools/.

key_points.point: The document demonstrates the utility of AI agents in automating labor-intensive research and evaluation tasks. By using an AI agent to process over 1000 disclosures, the team significantly reduced the expert time required for systematic literature reviews and data analysis. This highlights the potential for AI to scale complex, high-value cognitive work.
key_points.verbatim: AI agents are increasingly deployed for complex research tasks, from systematic literature reviews to data analysis. Given the labor-intensive nature of manually collecting and acquiring over 1000 disclosures across multiple companies, which cumulatively consumes months of expert time from the FMTI team, we developed an automated evaluation agent to test whether language model-based AI agents could reliably assess company transparency at scale.

key_points.point: The document asserts that the inherent opacity of foundation model development, particularly regarding training data and compute, hinders external evaluation and accountability. It highlights that while companies disclose some capability evaluations, they provide limited methodological detail, preventing external reproduction or third-party assessment. This lack of transparency is framed as a critical information deficit that necessitates policy intervention.
key_points.verbatim: Companies are most opaque about their training data and training compute as well as the post-deployment usage and impact of their flagship models. While companies tend to disclose evaluations of model capabilities and risks, limited methodological transparency, third-party involvement, reproducibility, and reporting of train-test overlap pose challenges.

key_points.point: The document advocates for rigorous, reproducible benchmarking and standardized risk taxonomies to ensure model safety. By requiring developers to map post-training mitigations to specific risk categories, the framework aims to force accountability and technical precision in safety practices. This approach treats transparency as a prerequisite for effective alignment and risk management.
key_points.verbatim: The newest edition includes indicators asking the developer to taxonomize the capabilities optimized for during post-training, the risks considered while developing the model, and the mitigations implemented while developing the model.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the necessity of external, independent evaluation to verify developer claims regarding model risks and capabilities. It highlights the current lack of standardization and independence in contracted expert evaluations as a critical gap in the safety ecosystem. The proposed indicators aim to institutionalize safe-harbor policies for researchers to conduct good-faith audits.
key_points.verbatim: Developers frequently use contracted expert evaluators to uncover model risks (Longpre et al., 2025a) but there remains many uncertainties like the lack of standardization (Ruth E. Appel, 2024) and the amount of independence (Santeri Koivula & Alejandro Tlaie, 2025).

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the necessity of internal organizational transparency, such as disclosing development roadmaps and oversight structures, to mitigate risks associated with frontier model development. By tracking organizational practices alongside technical capabilities, it seeks to create a record of accountability that can inform safety assessments. This reflects a safetyist desire to move beyond superficial model-level metrics toward understanding the institutional processes governing AI safety.
key_points.verbatim: To build on this strength, we introduced new indicators to increase our focus on the companies themselves. In the upstream domain, we add an indicator about the developer’s organization structure, namely the internal organization chart of employees involved in foundation model development.

key_points.point: The document argues that transparency regarding security practices is essential and can be achieved without compromising the efficacy of those security measures. It critiques the tendency of companies like Anthropic and Google to justify opacity on security grounds, noting that these companies actually do disclose enough information to meet the index's security indicators. This aligns with safetyist intentions to mandate rigorous, verifiable security standards for frontier models.
key_points.verbatim: A common concern is that transparency into (cyber)security practices will undermine the very efficacy of those security practices. While there are complex tradeoffs in this space, we believe transparency at the level required by the relevant FMTI 2025 indicator can be achieved with minimal, if any, loss to security.

key_points.point: The document asserts that companies are less likely to disclose risk information than capabilities because reporting risks increases potential liability and the likelihood of lawsuits. This creates a systemic incentive for developers to prioritize commercial marketing over safety transparency, which safetyists argue necessitates external, mandatory oversight.
key_points.verbatim: Whereas companies often publish capabilities evaluation results to improve the commercial success of their models, reporting risks could increase liability and the likelihood of lawsuits from consumers and enterprises harmed by those risks.

key_points.point: The document highlights that companies frequently withhold information regarding compute, architecture, and training data, citing trade secrets and security risks. This inherent opacity, whether justified by competitive advantage or security, fundamentally hinders the ability of external stakeholders to assess systemic risks or verify safety claims. The document notes that even when companies provide justifications, the lack of granular data prevents independent verification of safety-critical model properties.
key_points.verbatim: The benefit of potentially exposing specific numbers is outweighed by the risk of disclosure of trade secrets, and relatedly, the risk of potential security vulnerabilities through reverse engineering.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 5, FMTI disclosures that demonstrate regress and progress

key_points.point: The document supports the EU AI Act's requirement for public summaries of training data as a necessary step toward transparency. By mandating disclosure of training content, the policy aims to mitigate risks associated with data poisoning and harmful model behaviors. This aligns with the safetyist goal of ensuring that the foundational elements of AGI development are subject to public scrutiny and regulatory oversight.
key_points.verbatim: The EU AI Act mandates that foundation model developers make available to the public a summary of the training data they use. This legal requirement is mandatory for developers irrespective of whether they choose onto the Code of Practice, and irrespective of whether their models are designating as posing systemic risk.

key_points.point: The document emphasizes the necessity of rigorous, third-party evaluation and incident reporting systems to manage risks from general-purpose AI. By citing frameworks for adverse event reporting and flaw disclosure, the text supports the safetyist position that deployment must be accompanied by verifiable safety mechanisms. This reflects a commitment to proactive risk management over unchecked scaling.

key_points.point: The FMTI team maintains human oversight by ensuring that all final scores are determined by human judgment rather than the AI agent. The agent serves as a high-speed data processor that assists the team, but the final accountability remains with human experts who validate the findings through engagement with the companies.
key_points.verbatim: All scores published in the 2025 FMTI reflect the FMTI team’s judgments, with multiple steps of validation including engagement with the companies, and none of the published scores were proposed or directly determined by any AI system.

key_points.point: The authors advocate for more aggressive policy intervention to address information deficits, specifically regarding the downstream impact of models on the economy and society. They emphasize that current market forces are insufficient to drive transparency, implying that mandatory disclosure requirements are necessary to hold companies accountable for their practices.
key_points.verbatim: For many of these specific topics, we do not currently expect transparency to improve based on current market forces, which warrants consideration of whether policy intervention is desirable to address information deficits.

key_points.point: The index explicitly tracks environmental impacts, including energy and water usage for training runs, mirroring the logic of industrial reporting. By including these as key indicators, the authors treat AI development as a resource-intensive industrial process that requires public oversight.
key_points.verbatim: The compute subdomain covers indicators like the amount of hardware used to train a model, the owner of that hardware, the associated computational cost and training duration, and resulting energy and environmental impacts of using that compute to build the model.

key_points.point: The document highlights the significant environmental costs of AI development, specifically noting the consumption of energy, water, and electricity. It frames these computational costs as a divisive topic due to their impact on national-level resource allocation. This aligns with skeptic concerns regarding the unsustainable resource footprint of large-scale model training.
key_points.verbatim: For this reason, the environmental impact of AI and its accurate measurement has become an increasingly divisive topic, especially as the computational costs of AI may substantively influence national-level resource allocation of energy, water, and electricity.

key_points.point: The document notes the growing reliance on human data labor, which raises significant human rights and labor protection concerns. It identifies a trend of companies acquiring or partnering with data labor firms, suggesting that the 'intelligence' of these models is built upon a foundation of potentially exploited human work. This supports the skeptic view that AI progress is inextricably linked to labor displacement and poor working conditions.
key_points.verbatim: Human data labor is an established area of advocacy on human rights, especially given human-produced training data may specifically be used to address model behaviors related to risky tendencies (Al Hammada, 2024).

key_points.point: The document asserts that AI developers are highly opaque regarding the environmental costs of model training, specifically energy and water consumption. It highlights that even the largest tech companies fail to disclose these metrics, suggesting that the ecological footprint of AI is being systematically hidden from public view. This lack of disclosure hinders the ability to assess the true sustainability of the current AI development trajectory.
key_points.verbatim: Companies are highly opaque about the environmental impact of building foundation models. 10 companies disclose none of the key information related to environmental impact: AI21 Labs, Alibaba, Amazon, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Google, Midjourney, Mistral, OpenAI, and xAI.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 5.1, There is little to no information on the environmental impact of AI.

key_points.point: The document supports the use of tiered, systematic auditing of AI models to address the wide variance in transparency practices across the industry. By scoring developers on 100 indicators, it demonstrates that transparency is an organizational choice rather than a technical constraint, justifying the need for standardized, mandatory reporting requirements to ensure accountability across all developers.
key_points.verbatim: This range suggests that organizational choice is a core factor in upstream transparency. Current conditions in the ecosystem neither compel companies to demonstrate non-zero transparency nor prevent them from achieving very high levels of transparency.

key_points.point: The document implicitly supports the view that open weights do not equate to transparency, as evidenced by the fact that some open-weight developers score poorly on upstream transparency indicators. It highlights that technical release strategies are distinct from the disclosure of training data, compute usage, and organizational oversight, which are necessary for genuine transparency.
key_points.verbatim: Even excluding these three companies, Figure 8 shows that for every large subdomain of the upstream domain, at least one company scores 0% while another scores 90%. This range suggests that organizational choice is a core factor in upstream transparency.

key_points.point: The document explicitly distinguishes between 'openness' (releasing weights) and 'transparency' (public access to information), noting that high-profile open model developers like Meta, Alibaba, and DeepSeek are often quite opaque. This confirms the skeptic belief that open weights do not automatically equate to genuine corporate transparency or accountability.
key_points.verbatim: The 2025 FMTI demonstrates the bifurcation among open developers: some developers clearly prioritize transparency (i.e. AI21 Labs, IBM; average = 82.5) with an average score more than 3 times that of their counterparts (i.e. Alibaba, DeepSeek, Meta; average = 25.3). These results confirm that while openness and transparency may correlate, they are meaningfully distinct.

key_points.point: The document highlights that current environmental disclosures are incomplete because they focus on average input-output interactions rather than the cumulative costs of model training and total usage. This supports the skeptic view that companies obscure the true environmental and resource footprint of their AI systems.
key_points.verbatim: However, this is incomplete: it does not provide information on the impact of model training and is insufficient for understanding the cumulative costs of model use, since most companies do not release information about the total amount of usage.

key_points.point: The document demonstrates that company-prepared reports are significantly more comprehensive than those prepared by external teams, suggesting that voluntary disclosure is insufficient for accountability. It advocates for standardized, rigorous reporting requirements that force companies to disclose non-public information, such as organizational charts and specific risk evaluation results. This supports the skeptic view that independent, mandatory auditing is required to overcome corporate tendencies toward opacity.
key_points.verbatim: FMTI-prepared reports score around half that of company-prepared reports. There are two ways in which the reports are initially prepared: by the developers and by the FMTI team.
key_points.excerpt_context: Section 5, FMTI-prepared reports vs company-prepared reports

key_points.point: The document identifies a systemic industry-wide decline in transparency, with companies regressing on disclosures regarding compute, energy usage, and model behavior. It argues that policy interventions, such as the EU AI Act, are essential to reverse this trend. By aligning FMTI indicators with regulatory templates, the authors intend to create a feedback loop where legal obligations drive measurable improvements in public-facing transparency.
key_points.verbatim: The 2025 FMTI demonstrates significant and systemic opacity across almost all foundation model developers on training data transparency, which has been throughout the history of the FMTI.

key_points.point: The document includes multiple references to the environmental and labor costs of AI, such as energy consumption and the exploitation of data workers. By highlighting research on carbon emissions and the conditions of workers in the Global South, the text validates the skeptic concern that AI's 'progress' is built upon hidden, measurable harms. This supports the argument that AI development must be scrutinized for its real-world social and ecological footprint.

key_points.point: The document acknowledges that automated agents can produce false positives and miss information compared to human researchers. This underscores the necessity of human review in auditing processes, as the agent's verbosity and retrieval limitations can lead to inaccurate assessments if not carefully monitored.
key_points.verbatim: We noticed that the agent’s outputs are much more verbose than the FMTI team’s transparency report, increasing the scope for false positives (irrelevant information surfaced during the search).

factual_claims.claim: The average transparency score of foundation model developers fell from 58 in 2024 to 40 in 2025, reversing the progress made between 2023 and 2024.

factual_claims.claim: The 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index (FMTI) has undergone a major revision, introducing 55 new indicators while retaining only 9 from the previous year. This reflects a shift toward more specific, reproducible, and granular transparency requirements for foundation model developers.
The average score for the 2025 Foundation Model Transparency Index is 40.69 out of 100, indicating a generally poor state of transparency across the AI ecosystem.

evidence_criteria.category_criteria: Empirical measurement of transparency across 13 developers based on 100 indicators.

factual_claims.claim: Automated agents using LLMs can effectively augment human teams in transparency evaluation, though they require human verification to avoid false positives and negatives.

factual_claims.claim: IBM and Writer are the only companies that disclose the total monetary cost of building their flagship foundation models, which is essential for calculating return on investment and understanding AI supply chain economics.

evidence_criteria.category_criteria: Empirical claim based on index audit data.

factual_claims.claim: The average score for FMTI-prepared transparency reports is approximately half that of company-prepared reports, indicating that companies possess significant non-public information that is not captured by external analysis.

factual_claims.claim: There is a systemic decline in transparency among major foundation model developers, with 7 out of 9 companies tracked across 2024 and 2025 showing lower transparency scores in the latter year.

The AI industry is increasingly adopting formal data licensing agreements with content providers to secure training data, as evidenced by deals between major AI labs and publishers like News Corp and Reddit.
The FMTI team developed an automated evaluation agent using Claude 4 to assess company transparency across 100 indicators, utilizing web search and PDF extraction tools.
